# County Socioeconomic Status and Premature Mortality from Cancer in the United States

**Authors:** Aleah L. Thomas; Rachel J. Kulchar; Erica S. Stephens; Lee Mason; Sarah S. Jackson; Alexandra R. Harris; Aldenise P. Ewing; Meredith S Shiels; Catherine M. Pichardo; Jennifer K. McGee-Avila; Wayne R. Lawrence

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Rockville, MD, USA | 2Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, NY, USA | 3Salivary Disorders Unit, National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA | 4School of Dentistry, University of California Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California, USA | 5Division of Epidemiology, College of Public Health, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA | 6Division of Cancer Control and Population Sciences, NCI, NIH, Rockville, Maryland

## Abstract

There are consistent data demonstrating socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with cancer survivorship among older adults, but research on the relationship between area-level SES and risk of premature mortality from cancer remains not well understood. This study investigated the association between county-level SES and premature mortality from cancer.

Demographic characteristics and causes of death were ascertained from the national death certificate data for years 2016–2020. Premature cancer death was defined as cancer mortality between ages 25–64. County SES was calculated using the Yost Index and categorized into distribution-based quintiles (1=lowest SES, 5=highest SES). To calculate the mortality-adjusted rate ratios (aRR) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95%CI) for the associations between county SES and cancer, we performed multivariable linear mixed models, adjusting for confounders.

A total of 3,143 counties were included. The age-adjusted mortality rates of all cancers combined were 107.6, 98.4, 88.6, 81.1, and 66.7 per 100,000 population for the 5 SES quintiles, respectively. Compared with high SES counties, low SES counties had a 58% greater premature cancer mortality rate (aRRquintile 1 vs. 5=1.58, 95%CI: 1.55–1.60). Similar associations were observed when stratified by sex, though risk was greatest among men ([aRRwomen=1.58, 95%CI: 1.55–1.60]; [aRRmen=1.66, 95%CI: 1.62–1.70]). Among leading cancer types, the association was greatest for lung cancer mortality for the lowest SES counties (aRR=2.03; 95%CI: 1.98–2.08).

Our findings demonstrate that lower SES counties are at greater risk of premature mortality from cancer. Place-based interventions should target the socioeconomic environment across the cancer control continuum.

## Introduction

Cancer is the second leading cause of mortality in United States (U.S.) and the leading cause of death among individuals aged 45–64 years (1). The economic burden of cancer between 2020 and 2050 is estimated to exceed 5 trillion dollars in the U.S., one of the highest costs among all countries globally (2). Premature cancer deaths can further impact the economy through substantial productivity declines attributed to years of lost life in comparison to cancer deaths at older age (3). Previous studies have suggested an association between county socioeconomic status (SES) and cancer mortality (4,5). However, understanding of the contribution of low county SES to premature mortality from cancer remains limited. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the associations between county SES and risk of premature mortality from cancer.

## Methods

We obtained information about demographic characteristics and underlying causes of death from death certificate data compiled by the National Center for Health Statistics from January 2016 to December 2020. Deaths were categorized based on International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes by Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results (SEER) Cause of Death Recodes (6). Premature death from cancer was defined as cancer mortality between ages 25–64 years, aligning with prior studies (6,9). The study focused on overall and sex-specific cancer mortality and leading cancer type causes of death that were calculable among those <65 years of age (female breast, colon and rectum [colorectal], Corpus and Uterus, NOS [uterine], liver and intrahepatic bile duct, lung and bronchus, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, ovary, pancreas, prostate) (7,8) (Supplemental Table 1). National Institutes of Health Institutional Review Board waived approval and informed consent because the study used publicly available deidentified data. This study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guidelines (10).

County-level SES was measured using the Yost Index (11). This index is based on seven measures obtained from the 2016–2020 American Community Survey including percent below 150% of poverty line, median household income, median house value, median rent, percent working class, percent unemployed, and Education Index (percent with less than high school graduate, high school only and more than high school among ages ≥25 years). Higher scores indicated higher county-level SES. We further categorized scores into quintiles (1=lowest SES and 5=highest SES) based on the population distribution. The American Community Survey is a nationwide survey by the U.S. Census Bureau that collects annual information about the population (12).

Rurality of counties was based on the Rural-Urban Continuum Codes developed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture and grouped as nonmetropolitan and metropolitan counties (13). The percentage of non-White residents (continuous) and percentage of uninsured adults under the age of 65 (continuous) were obtained at the county-level derived from the 2020 American Community Survey.

A total of 3,143 counties and county-equivalents (representing ~99% of the total US) with reported cancer deaths were categorized into SES quintiles (county population median: 15,072.5). Age-adjusted premature cancer mortality rates by county SES were calculated. All rates were age standardized in five-year age groups to the 2000 U.S. population. Age-standardized death rates from 2016 to 2020 were used to compare premature mortality rates overall and by leading causes of cancer death. Cancer mortality-adjusted rate ratios (aRR) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI) of each quintile group compared with the fifth quintile (highest SES) group were calculated using multilevel linear mixed modeling on age-adjusted mortality weighted by county population, clustered at the state level, and adjusting for metropolitan status, percentage of uninsured adults (continuous), and percentage of non-White population (continuous). Likelihood ratio test was performed to assess model fit (P<0.05), and Q-Q plots were used to assess the normality of residuals. P for trend was calculated by modeling quintiles of county SES as a continuous variable. Analyses were conducted using SAS version 9.4.

## Results

Compared to the highest SES counties (Quintile 5), lower SES counties were clustered in the Appalachian and Southern regions (Figure 1). The age-adjusted premature mortality rates from all cancers combined were 107.6, 98.4, 88.6, 81.1, and 66.7 per 100,000 population from the first to the fifth SES quintiles, respectively (P < 0.05 for trend) (Supplemental Figure 1). Comparable findings were observed when stratified by sex. Furthermore, largely across all leading cancer types, premature mortality from cancer increased as quintile of county SES decreased, with lung and bronchus cancer having the greatest age-adjusted mortality rate across all quintiles (Supplemental Figure 2).

Compared with the highest quintiles of county SES, the lowest SES quintiles had a 58% higher overall premature cancer mortality (aRR=1.58; 95%CI: 1.55–1.60) (Figure 2). The aRR for all cancers combined for men was 66% higher for counties in the lowest SES quintile compared with the highest SES quintile (aRR=1.66; 95%CI: 1.62–1.70). Similar results were observed among women where the aRR was 48% higher among those in the lowest SES quintile counties compared with the highest (aRR=1.48; 95%CI: 1.45–1.52).

When examined by leading cancer types, compared to counties in the highest SES quintile, the lowest SES quintile had a higher mortality rate for all cancer types with the highest for lung and bronchus cancer (aRR=2.03; 95%CI: 1.98–2.08), followed by liver and intrahepatic bile duct cancer (aRR=1.74; 95%CI: 1.64–1.91), and colorectal cancer (aRR=1.51; 95%CI: 1.47–1.56) (all P for trend <0.05) (Figure 3). This trend was consistent among sex-specific cancers including prostate cancer (aRR=1.74; 95%CI: 1.54–1.93), female breast cancer (aRR=1.29; 95%CI: 1.23–1.36), ovarian cancer (aRR=1.14; 95%CI 1.05–1.24), and uterine cancer (aRR=1.40, 95%CI: 1.26–1.55).

## Discussion

In this analysis, lower county SES was associated with higher premature mortality for all cancers combined among both men and women, and across leading cancer types during 2016–2020. Additionally, most cancer types showed significant trends across quintiles of county SES and higher premature mortality from cancer.

The impact of low county SES was more pronounced among men. This sex difference in cancer mortality was observed in prior epidemiologic studies among adults and potentially attributed to differential exposure to carcinogens (e.g., tobacco, occupational UV exposure), response to therapy, and biological differences (14–18). Our findings add to this literature by documenting sex differences in the rate for premature death due to cancer. Additionally, lower SES counties were more likely to be in the Southern and Appalachian Region, which consists of states that were late adopters or did not adopt the Affordable Care Act Medicaid Expansion. Studies suggest cancer patients in Medicaid expanded states were more likely to be screened for cancer, diagnosed at earlier stages, and have better cancer survival outcomes compared with non-expanded states (19), indicating a potential social and political determinant contributing to the observed regional premature cancer mortality disparities among screen-detectable cancers (20,21).

For all leading cancer types the aRRs were highest in lower SES counties, indicating greater risk of premature cancer mortality when compared to the most affluent counties. The mortality rate was greatest for lung and bronchus cancer among low SES counties compared with high SES counties. This is likely due to the accumulation of factors including higher prevalence of tobacco use, greater exposure to ambient air pollution, and lower access to quality lung cancer treatment (22–25). Low SES counties have a greater proportion of underinsured people and experience greater barriers in accessing lung cancer care (e.g., screening, timely treatment). For instance, prior studies report individuals residing in more socioeconomically disadvantaged areas are less likely to utilize lung cancer screening, which suggests systemic disparities in access to preventative services (26,27). Additionally, studies have documented that residing in a socioeconomically disadvantaged neighborhood is associated with lower likelihood of receiving routine care, posing a greater challenge to receiving preventative health services (28). Further investigation is imperative to understand the numerous contributors to premature mortality from lung cancer among low SES counties to inform opportunities for place-based interventions.

Following lung and bronchus cancer, liver and intrahepatic bile duct cancer and colorectal cancers had the highest mortality rates. Studies have reported socioeconomic contributors to disparities in liver cancer risk and subsequent mortality (29). For instance, chronic hepatitis B and C infections are the main contributors to the most common form of liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma (30–33). Persons from communities that are socioeconomically disadvantaged encounter barriers in accessing curative HCV treatment, particularly the Medicaid-insured (30–37). Additional factors include a disproportionate burden of heavy alcohol consumption, tobacco use, and obesity among individuals that reside in low SES communities (38–40), all modifiable risk factors associated with liver and colorectal cancer incidence (33,41). Commercial determinants, which involve tactics employed by the private sector to encourage products and behaviors that negatively impact health (40), likely contribute to higher rates of liver and intrahepatic bile duct cancer and colorectal cancer incidence due to greater density of alcohol outlets, tobacco retailers, and fast-food restaurants in low SES counties compared with high SES counties (38–40). Additionally, prior studies have documented areas that are more socioeconomically disadvantaged have a lower prevalence of adherence to recommended cancer screening because of barriers to accessing medical care, more likely to present with late-stage disease at diagnosis, thus contributing to elevated risk of premature death from cancer (36, 41, 43–46).

Several limitations must be noted. First, because of the cross-sectional study design, we were unable to establish causality or the direct association. Second, we were unable to adjust for cancer risk factors, such as cigarette smoking, hence cofounding arising from these variables were not accounted for. Third, the Yost Index does not account for the full spectrum of socioeconomic measures (e.g., cost of living) (6,47). Finally, individual-level inferences cannot be made due to the ecological design.

## Conclusion

The findings of this ecological study suggest an association between low SES counties and increased risk of premature mortality from cancer, highlighting opportunities for place-based interventions to address socioeconomic disparities across the cancer control continuum. Future studies are needed to confirm our findings using individual-level data to inform public health policy and develop tailored cancer prevention interventions.
